title: Informative images need meaningful alternatives
text: An informative image needs a text alternative that communicates its purpose or meaning in context. A literal inventory of visible objects may miss the information the image conveys. The author must decide whether the image contributes information or only decoration.

title: Decorative images and empty alt attributes
text: For decorative HTML images that add no information, use an empty alt attribute so assistive technology can skip them. Missing the attribute is different from explicitly setting it empty. Whether an image is decorative depends on its role and surrounding content.

title: Text contrast thresholds and exceptions
text: WCAG 2.2 criterion 1.4.3 requires at least 4.5:1 contrast for ordinary text and 3:1 for qualifying large text. It includes exceptions for incidental text and logotypes. Apply the relevant definitions before flagging a design; checking one contrast ratio does not establish overall accessibility conformance.

title: Communicating information beyond colour
text: WCAG 2.2 criterion 1.4.1 addresses information communicated only through colour. Add an appropriate label, shape, pattern, or other visual distinction when colour identifies a status or action. Colour can still be used when the meaning is also available through another visual cue.

title: Stable organisational voice and adaptable tone
text: The Home Office describes its organisational voice as consistent across services while tone changes with the communication channel and user need. Its examples include direct task instructions and conversational internal support. This demonstrates why brand checks should consider channel context instead of enforcing the same wording everywhere.

title: Plain language for the intended audience
text: Digital.gov encourages familiar, clear wording and avoidance of acronyms or jargon that the audience may not understand. This is a useful pattern for an organisation to adopt in its own writing policy, rather than an automatic ban on specialist vocabulary in every context.

title: Headlines should convey context without overpromising
text: Digital.gov asks headlines to make sense independently, include important context, and avoid misleading promises. Its guide uses sentence case for titles and paragraph headings. The casing convention belongs to that publisher and should become a brand rule only when explicitly adopted.

title: Brand-specific clear-space measurement
text: The Chicago Bears guideline defines clear space around its Bear Head mark as at least one quarter of the mark's height. This is a concrete example of a measurable asset rule. The value belongs to that brand and must not be assumed to apply to the fictional demo logo.

title: Minimum logo size and approved alternatives
text: The Chicago Bears guidance gives its Bear Head mark a minimum reproduction width of half an inch or 35 digital pixels, and identifies the C mark for smaller applications. This illustrates asset-specific minimum sizes and alternate versions; it grants no right to use those marks.
